question: What is the prior art in source-traceable technical explainers, meaning slide decks, diagrams and explainer pages whose claims can each be traced back to a source such as code, configuration, a specification or a commit? Cover Slidev, Marp, Mermaid and other diagrams generated from code: how each keeps content tied to its source, how drift between the explainer and its source is detected, and where each falls short. Also cover how a team can honestly measure that a reader understood a technical change in about three minutes: comprehension measures such as recall questions, teach-back, task-based checks and think-aloud, how to avoid relying on self-reported understanding or reading time alone, sample sizes, timing, and known pitfalls. Prefer published studies, official documentation and source repositories.
summary: Technical presentations built from code (Slidev, Marp, Mermaid, PlantUML, etc.) are typically version-controlled text (Markdown or DSL), so content can live alongside source code. Slidev can include external code snippets and render Mermaid/PlantUML diagrams via servers【42†L101-L109】【47†L154-L162】. Marp itself has no built-in Mermaid support – diagrams must be pre-rendered or processed via CLI engines (e.g. Kroki) because Marp relies on server-side rendering【27†L12-L20】【72†L178-L186】. Mermaid and PlantUML promote the “diagram-as-code” approach: diagrams are just text, stored and reviewed with code so they “never drift out of date”【39†L6-L10】【37†L120-L128】. Drift between docs and code must be caught with external tools or processes (e.g. docdiff flags docs stale if code changes【35†L199-L207】). To measure rapid comprehension of a technical change, teams should use objective user-testing methods: ask users to paraphrase key points immediately, or perform a relevant task while thinking aloud【81†L192-L194】【79†L92-L99】. Success is judged by accuracy and speed, not by self-reported understanding or reading time【18†L192-L200】【55†L25-L34】. Small, iterative tests (often ~5–8 users) usually suffice【60†L75-L84】【62†L106-L113】.

findings.claim: Slidev slides are plain Markdown; developers can import live code from source files via <<< @/ path/to/file.js so slide content always reflects the current code【42†L101-L109】.

In Slidev, fenced Mermaid blocks are automatically converted to diagrams at build time【24†L230-L238】, and PlantUML blocks are rendered by sending code to PlantUML’s server by default (configurable via plantUmlServer)【47†L154-L162】.

Marp (Markdown Presentations) does not natively render Mermaid: a mermaid block appears as literal code unless the diagram is pre-rendered or passed through a CLI engine【27†L12-L20】. The Marp team notes that Marp Core “does not support mermaid.js” (since it is SSR-based), and recommends using an external rendering service (like Kroki) for Mermaid diagrams【72†L178-L186】【72†L194-L198】.

Mermaid’s design motto is “diagrams as code”: “Your diagram is just text… The diagram lives next to the thing it describes — and never drifts out of date”【39†L6-L10】. This means Mermaid source is version-controlled alongside system code.

PlantUML likewise treats diagrams as code: a .puml file is kept in the source repo and regenerated by CI. According to PlantUML docs, the diagram “cannot silently drift out of date on some wiki nobody edits, because it is part of the change set”【37†L120-L128】. Version-control and CI building ensure diagrams stay synced with code.
findings.quote: cannot silently drift out of date on some wiki nobody edits, because it is part of the change set

findings.claim: Tools exist to detect drift between code and documentation: e.g. docdiff lets developers annotate code with @doc links, then flags docs as stale if related code changes without updating them【35†L199-L207】. This ensures no claims in slides/docs are left unreviewed after code evolves.

Comprehension depends on user background, so it must be tested empirically (not just by readability formulas). Nielsen Norman notes that factors like IQ and education matter, so one “must test with real users” from the target audience to measure understanding【50†L108-L112】.

A cloze test (fill-in-the-blank) is one empirical measure: if participants fill ≥60% of missing words correctly, the text is deemed “reasonably comprehensible” to that audience【50†L124-L132】. This sets a benchmark for quick comprehension.

Immediately after reading, ask users to paraphrase or “teach back” the content. For example: “In your own words, what does this mean?”【81†L192-L194】. If they can restate the key meaning, it proves they built the intended understanding【79†L92-L99】.

Use task-based checks: have users perform a relevant task based on the change and observe success. Task-based comprehension is defined as “whether the user acts correctly on what they understood”【79†L92-L99】. If the user completes the task as intended (per pre-written criteria), they have likely understood the material.
findings.quote: whether the user acts correctly on what they understood

findings.claim: Observe users via think-aloud protocol to catch hidden misunderstandings. By verbalizing thoughts, users expose any “misconceptions” about the content【62†L97-L105】. This qualitative insight often reveals exactly which part of the explanation was unclear. (Think-aloud tests require only a few participants to yield actionable findings【62†L106-L113】.)

Measure performance (speed and accuracy) not just declared understanding. Real comprehension shows up in how quickly and correctly users act, not in click analytics or self-reports【52†L90-L99】【52†L106-L108】. For example, one practitioner notes that if ≥90% of users complete a task in ~3–4 minutes with minimal errors, comprehension is likely high【52†L90-L99】.

Avoid self-report and time proxies. Studies show self-reported reading time greatly overestimates actual time (by ~4× in one trial) and correlates poorly with comprehension【18†L192-L200】. Likewise, natural clickstream reading times have no meaningful correlation with text comprehension【55†L25-L34】. Relying on subjective or time-based metrics alone is therefore misleading.

Use iterative small-sample testing. For rapid validation, only a handful of users (often ~5–8) are needed per round【60†L75-L84】【62†L106-L113】. Multiple small rounds (testing, revising, retesting) catch recurring confusion faster than a single large test【60†L75-L84】.

No evidence was found of any slide/diagram tool automatically detecting drift or mismatches between slide content and code beyond using general version-control or external tools. In practice, teams must audit changes manually or use annotations (as in docdiff) to avoid stale content.

It is assumed (but not documented) that other diagrams-as-code tools (e.g. Graphviz, D2, etc.) follow similar patterns of living in repos; we did not find specific claims on their drift-detection features.
